title: Kagi Brings Back Old-School Search, One Human-Made Website at a Time
gist: A hands-on look at Kagi, a paid privacy-focused search engine ($5/month for 300 searches, $10/month unlimited, 100-search free trial) that runs its own web and news indexes and strips promoted results. Kagi has expanded beyond search into a 'Small Web' project curating human-made sites plus new Android and iOS apps, positioning explicitly against a web the author says AI is working to make unnecessary.

insights.claim: Kagi charges $5 a month plus sales tax for 300 searches including its standard-level AI assistant, $10 a month for unlimited searches and more AI assistant tokens, with a free trial covering 100 searches.
insights.speaker: David Nield
insights.so_what: Concrete price points for consumer paid search — the benchmark against which any subscription-search entrant will be measured.

insights.claim: Kagi's core argument is that searching the web always has a cost and the only question is the currency: dollars paid directly, data given up about online activity, or attention spent sifting through ads and sponsored links.
insights.speaker: David Nield
insights.so_what: A clean framing of the ad-versus-subscription tradeoff that any consumer software business monetizing attention must eventually answer.
insights.locator: The argument that Kagi puts forward for why you should pay

insights.claim: Kagi maintains its own indexes for web and news rather than reselling another engine's results, and tunes them to promote noncommercial sites and results uninfluenced by paid promotion or Google's shifting business practices.
insights.speaker: David Nield
insights.so_what: Owning the index is what makes an independent search economics story credible — without it a paid engine is just a reskin with a subscription attached.

insights.claim: Searching Kagi for a band returns the official website, Wikipedia page, social accounts and YouTube channel with no promoted results, related searches or sponsored content such as concert tickets — the pre-monetization result layout.
insights.speaker: David Nield
insights.so_what: Illustrates concretely what removing commercial intent layers from search results looks like, which is the product Kagi is actually selling.
insights.locator: For me, it feels a little bit like stepping back in time

insights.claim: Kagi's Small Web project curates human-made and human-curated sites with a StumbleUpon-style Next Post random-jump button, favoriting, search, sharing, and topic categories including DIY & Making, Travel & Outdoors, Retro and Pop Culture — explicitly modeled on old AltaVista and Yahoo directories.
insights.speaker: David Nield
insights.so_what: A search company building a human-curation layer is a hedge against its own index being flooded by generated content — watch whether rivals copy it.
insights.quote: dominated by algorithms, ads, and AI-generated noise,

insights.claim: Kagi has expanded beyond search into offering access to a multitude of AI models and recently launched apps for Android and iOS.
insights.speaker: David Nield
insights.so_what: Kagi is bundling model access with search under one subscription — the same bundling logic incumbents are using, executed from a paid-privacy position.
insights.locator: The company offers access to a multitude of AI models

insights.claim: The author argues that after decades of monetization creeping across search results, forums, social media and news outlets, AI is now actively removing the need for the open web altogether.
insights.speaker: David Nield
insights.so_what: If AI answers replace site visits, the entire ad-funded publishing economy loses its traffic base — the structural shift behind every publisher's current strategy scramble.
insights.locator: In the decades since those formative years

insights.claim: A market of companies is forming specifically to restore the spirit of the pre-monetization web, with Kagi as a named participant expanding from a Google-alternative search tool into curation of human-written sites.
insights.speaker: David Nield
insights.so_what: Human-authored provenance is emerging as a paid product category — a possible scarcity premium as generated content saturates the index.
insights.locator: There are now a good number of companies that are keen

insights.claim: Browsing the Small Web surfaced niche human-written blog posts on Python nuances, particle physics and the art of storytelling — content created for creativity's sake rather than to go viral or generate revenue.
insights.speaker: David Nield
insights.so_what: The non-commercial corpus is exactly the material AI training pipelines have consumed but ad-driven search stopped surfacing — a contested resource.
insights.locator: You shouldn’t expect to turn up treasure with every click
